title: How to Move AI Agent Reads Off the Salesforce API Before HPI Metering
summary: A six-step plan to move AI agent reads from Salesforce MCP and APIs to a synced Postgres or warehouse copy, so read traffic stops counting as HPIs.
body_markdown:
## How do you move agent reads off the Salesforce API?


**Short answer:** Measure which records your agents read, sync those objects into Postgres or a warehouse, and give the agent a read-only SQL tool in place of its Salesforce read tools. Keep writes on Salesforce. Run both paths side by side until the answers match, then switch. Reads against your own database never reach Salesforce, so they never become Headless Platform Interactions (HPIs), the per-call unit Salesforce plans to bill in Flex Credits.


*Written for the rules Salesforce has announced as of October 24, 2026. Metering hasn't started, and Salesforce promises 30 days' notice.*


## Why should reads move first?


Agents read far more than they write. A pipeline review, an account brief, or a churn scan can run five or ten queries and change nothing. Once metering starts, Salesforce charges each successful call from a registered agent the same flat rate, whether it reads one field or creates a record.


-


**Reads drive most of the bill.** In the example from our[cost-cutting guide](https://www.stacksync.com/blog/reduce-salesforce-mcp-costs-ai-agents) , 8 of 10 calls in a typical request are reads.


-


**Reads hit hard limits.** The hosted MCP` soqlQuery` tool caps at 50,000 records per transaction and` find` at 2,000. A database has no such cap.


-


**Reads are easy to move.** A read has no side effects, so a wrong answer from the new path costs you a retry, not bad data.


Switching the agent from MCP to the REST API saves nothing. Salesforce meters registered agent calls on both. The only read that costs no HPI is one that doesn't reach Salesforce.


## Step 1: Which records do your agents read?


Run each agent workflow 20 times in a sandbox, where Salesforce doesn't meter calls, and log every tool call. For each call, record the tool, the object, the fields, and whether it read or wrote.


Workflow Read calls Write calls Objects read


Account brief 6 0 Account, Contact, Opportunity, Task


Pipeline review 4 0 Opportunity, OpportunityLineItem, User


Renewal follow-up 5 2 Account, Opportunity, Contract


Example inventory. Replace with your own sandbox logs.


The objects that show up in most read calls are your first sync scope. In most CRM agents, that is Account, Contact, Opportunity, and activity history.


## Step 2: What should you sync?


Sync the objects from step 1 with every field the agent reads, plus the IDs that join them:` AccountId` ,` OwnerId` ,` ContactId` . Add` LastModifiedDate` so the agent can tell how recent a record is.


Then decide who can see what. Salesforce enforces field-level security and sharing rules on every MCP call. A database copy holds whatever the sync's integration user can see. If one agent serves many reps, rebuild access in the database: a view per role, or Postgres row-level security keyed on` OwnerId` or territory. Skip this and a rep can ask the agent about accounts they can't open in Salesforce.


The new read path, layer by layer


## Step 3: How do you set up the sync?


Connect Salesforce and the database in Stacksync, pick the objects and fields, and run the backfill. After that, Stacksync keeps both systems in two-way sync: a change in Salesforce lands in Postgres, and a change in Postgres lands in Salesforce, with write permissions you set per field. See[Salesforce to Postgres two-way sync](https://www.stacksync.com/crm/salesforce-postgres-bidirectional-sync) .


-


**Run it as an integration.** Give the sync its own integration user and connected app, separate from every agent. That keeps it on the traditional-integration side of Salesforce's line. The[Agentic Identity checklist](https://www.stacksync.com/blog/salesforce-agentic-identity-checklist) explains why the split matters.


-


**Budget its API calls.** The sync counts against your org's daily API request limit. Stacksync batches record changes and lets you set a rate ceiling per app, so the sync stays inside the budget you give it.


-


**Keep the database read-only to agents** at this stage. Grant the agent's database role` SELECT` only.


## Step 4: How does the agent query the database?


Replace the agent's Salesforce read tools with one SQL tool. You can expose it through a Postgres MCP server or as a function in your agent harness. Either way:


-


Connect with the read-only role from step 3, pointed at the access-controlled views, not the raw tables.


-


Put the table and column list in the system prompt, so the agent doesn't spend turns discovering schema.


-


Set a statement timeout and a row limit, so a bad query fails fast instead of scanning millions of rows.


-


Remove` soqlQuery` ,` find` , and` getRelatedRecords` from the agent, or move it from` sobject-all` to` sobject-mutations` for writes only. The[endpoint guide](https://www.stacksync.com/blog/salesforce-mcp-server-endpoints-tools) lists what each server exposes.


A join that took four MCP calls becomes one query. You can also join CRM data with billing, product usage, or ERP tables that Salesforce never held.


## Step 5: Where do writes go?


Leave writes on Salesforce for now. The cleanest pattern is one Flow published as a custom MCP tool per business action, such as "Log renewal follow-up." Each one costs one HPI and runs your validation rules.


Writing to Postgres and letting the sync carry the change back also works, since the sync is two-way. Salesforce hasn't published how it classifies agent activity that reaches Salesforce through a sync. Get a written answer from your account executive before you move writes. Until then, treat the database as the read path.
